subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Monday, week eleven. A client emailed Himani one line, 'Please recheck this,' and she spent the evening sure she'd be let go. Pallavi, her flatmate, listened, then said, 'What have you actually done since you joined? Write it down. Not feelings. Things.'
Thursday. Himani opened a note on her phone called 'Facts'. She typed slowly: fixed the invoice bug that had been open for a year. Client in Pune said 'thank you, very clear'. Manager asked her to train the next intern. Finished the audit checklist two days early. Eleven lines by bedtime.
The next month, Friday. Her review draft said 'needs to speak up more'. The old voice started: see, they know. Himani stopped, opened 'Facts' and read it twice. Then she wrote one more line: one improvement point, among eleven good ones. That's normal. She didn't feel confident, exactly. But she didn't believe the voice either.

qa.q: What did Himani call the note on her phone?
What was Himani feeling when the review draft said she needed to speak up more?
qa.a: She felt the old fear that it proved she was failing, until she checked it against her list of facts.

qa.q: Which approach worked better for Himani than trying to feel confident, and why?
qa.a: Reading her list of completed work and positive feedback let her test the doubtful thought against facts, so the thought lost its grip.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel if she saw Himani's 'Facts' note a month later?
qa.a: Pallavi might feel glad and a little proud that Pallavi's simple suggestion is helping Himani handle doubt.

grounding: It shows a person keeping a list of completed work and good feedback and reading it when doubt spikes, testing the thought against facts.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Pranav, you look like I did at twenty-five. Come, your Ishita Bua will show you something.
This old diary? Open it. The back pages. See, 'Week 3: finished the tender file, boss said "neat work"'. 'Week 7: client from Nashik asked for me by name.' 'Week 12: made a mistake in the rates, fixed it same day, no loss.'
When I joined the engineering firm, I was the only woman on the site team and I thought every day that they'd made a mistake hiring me. My mind kept saying, you're a fraud. I tried telling myself to feel confident. It didn't work at all.
So I started writing facts at the back of my diary. When the fear came, I'd read them. Not to feel good. To check. Is 'fraud' true? The page said no.
You've done good things these three months, Pranav. Start your own list tonight.

qa.q: Who asked for Ishita by name in week seven?
qa.a: A client from Nashik asked for her by name.

qa.q: What did Ishita's mind keep telling her when she joined the firm?
qa.a: It kept telling her she was a fraud and that hiring her was a mistake, which left her afraid and doubting herself.

qa.q: What does Ishita advise Pranav to do, and why?
qa.a: She tells Pranav to start a list of facts tonight, so Pranav can check doubtful thoughts against evidence rather than just trying to feel confident.

qa.q: How might Pranav feel seeing his Bua's old diary pages?
qa.a: Pranav may feel less alone and more hopeful, seeing that someone Pranav respects had the same doubts and found a way through.

grounding: It shows an elder describing how she kept a record of completed work and feedback and read it when doubt rose, testing the thought against facts.
